specStatements.text: Plant and animal cells (eukaryotic cells) have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.

Bacterial cells (prokaryotic cells) are much smaller in comparison. They have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall. The genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. It is a single DNA loop and there may be one or more small rings of DNA called plasmids.
Students should be able to demonstrate an understanding of the scale and size of cells and be able to make order of magnitude calculations, including the use of standard form.

Students should be able to explain how the main sub-cellular structures, including the nucleus, cell membranes, mitochondria, chloroplasts in plant cells and plasmids in bacterial cells are related to their functions.
Most animal cells have the following parts: a nucleus; cytoplasm; a cell membrane; mitochondria; ribosomes.
In addition to the parts found in animal cells, plant cells often have: chloroplasts; a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap.
Plant and algal cells also have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell.
Students should be able to use estimations and explain what they should be used to judge the relative size or area of sub-cellular structures.

Students should be able to, when provided with appropriate information, explain how the structure of different types of cell relate to their function in a tissue, an organ or organ system, or the whole organism.
Cells may be specialised to carry out a particular function: sperm cells, nerve cells and muscle cells in animals; root hair cells, xylem and phloem cells in plants.
Students should be able to explain the importance of cell differentiation.

As an organism develops, cells differentiate to form different types of cells. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage.; Many types of plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.

In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement. As a cell differentiates it acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function. It has become a specialised cell.
Students should be able to: understand how microscopy techniques have developed over time; explain how electron microscopy has increased understanding of sub-cellular structures.
Limited to the differences in magnification and resolution.

An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope. This means that it can be used to study cells in much finer detail. This has enabled biologists to see and understand many more sub-cellular structures.
Students should be able to carry out calculations involving magnification, real size and image size using the formula:
magnification = (size of image) / (size of real object)
Students should be able to express answers in standard form if appropriate.
Bacteria multiply by simple cell division (binary fission) as often as once every 20 minutes if they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature.
Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth solution or as colonies on an agar gel plate.
Uncontaminated cultures of microorganisms are required for investigating the action of disinfectants and antibiotics.
Students should be able to describe how to prepare an uncontaminated culture using aseptic technique.

They should be able to explain why: Petri dishes and culture media must be sterilised before use; inoculating loops used to transfer microorganisms to the media must be sterilised by passing them through a flame; the lid of the Petri dish should be secured with adhesive tape and stored upside down; in school and college laboratories, cultures should be incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C.
Students should be able to calculate cross-sectional areas of colonies or clear areas around colonies using πr².
Students should be able to calculate the number of bacteria in a population after a certain time if given the mean division time.
Students should be able to express the answer in standard form.

scopeNotes.statement: Limited to the differences in magnification and resolution.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Microscopy is treated only through the differences in magnification and resolution between a light microscope and an electron microscope. No content is included on how an electron microscope works, on the different types of electron microscope, or on staining and specimen preparation.

concepts.definition: A cell that has its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic cells; they also have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.

A cell whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. Bacterial cells are prokaryotic cells: they have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall, they are much smaller than plant and animal cells, and their genetic material is a single DNA loop.
A small ring of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterial cell, separate from the single DNA loop. A bacterial cell may contain one or more plasmids.
The sub-cellular structure that encloses the genetic material of a plant or animal cell and controls the activities of the cell.
The structure that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell and controls the passage of substances into and out of the cell.
The jelly-like part of a cell in which most of the cell's chemical reactions take place and in which the sub-cellular structures are found.

Sub-cellular structures in which aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs to carry out its functions. Cells that need a great deal of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
Sub-cellular structures where protein synthesis takes place: amino acids are joined together to make the proteins the cell needs.

A sub-cellular structure found in plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll. The chlorophyll absorbs light so that the cell can carry out photosynthesis, so chloroplasts are found in plant cells that receive light rather than in every plant cell.
A space in the cytoplasm of a plant cell that is filled with cell sap. It is one of the parts plant cells often have in addition to the parts found in animal cells.
A layer made of cellulose that surrounds the cell membrane of plant and algal cells and strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
A cell whose structure enables it to carry out a particular function. Examples are sperm cells, nerve cells and muscle cells in animals, and root hair cells, xylem and phloem cells in plants.
A specialised plant cell in the root with a long, thin extension into the soil. The extension increases the surface area of the cell for absorbing water and mineral ions.

Specialised plant cells that form transport tissues. Xylem cells form hollow tubes with thickened walls that carry water and mineral ions from the roots; phloem cells form tubes with sieve plates that carry dissolved sugars through the plant.

The process in which a cell acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function, so that it becomes a specialised cell. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage, while many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
How many times larger an image is than the real object, calculated using magnification = size of image / size of real object. The image size and the real size must be measured in the same units.

The ability of a microscope to show two points that are close together as separate points. An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope, so it can be used to study cells in much finer detail.

The simple cell division by which bacteria multiply. If they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature, bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes, so the population doubles at each division.
The nutrients supplied for growing microorganisms. Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth solution, or as colonies on an agar gel plate.

The set of precautions used to prepare an uncontaminated culture. Petri dishes and culture media are sterilised before use; inoculating loops are sterilised by passing them through a flame; the lid of the Petri dish is secured with adhesive tape and the dish is stored upside down; and in school and college laboratories cultures are incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C.

A culture that contains only the microorganism being studied, with no microorganisms from the air, the skin or the apparatus. Uncontaminated cultures are required for investigating the action of disinfectants and antibiotics.

misconceptions.question: Where is the genetic material of a bacterial cell found?
misconceptions.correct: In the cytoplasm, as a single DNA loop, with one or more plasmids; it is not enclosed in a nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: A bacterial cell keeps its genetic material inside a nucleus, in the same way as a plant or animal cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet plant and animal cells first, where the nucleus is the most obvious structure, so they treat it as a part that every cell must have. Diagrams of bacteria often show the DNA loop as a dark region that looks like a nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: Bacterial cells (prokaryotic cells) have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall. The genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus: it is a single DNA loop and there may be one or more small rings of DNA called plasmids.

misconceptions.question: How does the size of a bacterial cell compare with the size of an animal cell?
misconceptions.correct: A bacterial cell is much smaller: it is around one micrometre across, while an animal cell is usually tens of micrometres across.
misconceptions.misconception: Bacterial cells are only a little smaller than animal cells, because both are drawn at about the same size.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams of bacterial cells and animal cells are each drawn to fill the space available, and are usually printed without a scale bar, so the difference in scale is hidden.
misconceptions.correction: Bacterial cells (prokaryotic cells) are much smaller in comparison with plant and animal cells. The difference is best shown by an order of magnitude calculation, using standard form.

misconceptions.question: Which is the larger length, 2 × 10⁻⁶ m or 6 × 10⁻⁵ m?
misconceptions.correct: 6 × 10⁻⁵ m, because 10⁻⁵ m is ten times larger than 10⁻⁶ m.
misconceptions.misconception: A more negative power of ten means a bigger number, so 2 × 10⁻⁶ m is larger than 6 × 10⁻⁵ m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the digits in the index (6 against 5) without taking the minus sign into account, and they are used to a bigger digit meaning a bigger number.
misconceptions.correction: In standard form the more negative the index, the smaller the number: 10⁻⁶ m is one tenth of 10⁻⁵ m. Order of magnitude calculations should be set out in standard form so that the powers of ten can be compared directly.

misconceptions.question: Which cells have a cell wall made of cellulose?
misconceptions.misconception: Any cell that needs support has a cellulose cell wall, so animal cells and bacterial cells have one as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a cell wall strengthens the cell and assume every cell needs strengthening. They also learn that bacterial cells have a cell wall, and assume that all cell walls must be made of the same material.
misconceptions.correction: Plant and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall. Bacterial cells are surrounded by a cell wall, but it is not made of cellulose.

misconceptions.question: Does every plant cell contain chloroplasts?
misconceptions.correct: No. Plant cells often have chloroplasts, but cells that receive no light, such as root hair cells, do not.
misconceptions.misconception: Every plant cell contains chloroplasts, because the whole plant carries out photosynthesis.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The plant cell in almost every diagram is a leaf cell packed with chloroplasts, so students treat chloroplasts as a defining feature of all plant cells rather than as a structure related to a function.
misconceptions.correction: In addition to the parts found in animal cells, plant cells often have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis, so cells that are not exposed to light do not contain them.

misconceptions.question: What do mitochondria do in a cell?
misconceptions.correct: Aerobic respiration takes place in mitochondria, transferring energy for the cell to use.
misconceptions.misconception: Mitochondria make the cell's energy and store it there until the cell needs it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mitochondria are often described as making or producing energy, and students have not yet separated the idea of energy being transferred from the idea of energy being created and stored.
misconceptions.correction: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place. Respiration transfers energy from glucose so that the cell can use it; the energy is not made in the mitochondria and is not stored there. Cells that need a great deal of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.

misconceptions.question: Which sub-cellular structure is the site of protein synthesis?
misconceptions.misconception: Ribosomes are where respiration takes place, and mitochondria are where the cell's proteins are made.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are small structures in the cytoplasm that are learned as a pair, and their names are unfamiliar, so students swap the two functions.
misconceptions.correction: Ribosomes are where protein synthesis takes place; mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place. Each of the main sub-cellular structures has to be related to its own function.

misconceptions.question: Do animal cells contain a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap?
misconceptions.correct: No. A permanent vacuole filled with cell sap is one of the parts found in plant cells.
misconceptions.misconception: Animal cells contain a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, just as plant cells do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The vacuole is such a large and prominent feature of the plant cell diagram that students remember it as a general part of any cell rather than as a plant cell feature.
misconceptions.correction: Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. In addition to these parts, plant cells often have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap.

misconceptions.question: What changes inside a cell as it becomes specialised?
misconceptions.correct: It acquires different sub-cellular structures that enable it to carry out a certain function.
misconceptions.misconception: A cell becomes specialised by growing bigger, while keeping exactly the same sub-cellular structures as before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Specialised cells are recognised in diagrams by their outline and size, so students focus on the shape of the cell rather than on the sub-cellular structures inside it.
misconceptions.correction: As a cell differentiates it acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function. It has become a specialised cell.

misconceptions.question: When are plant cells able to differentiate?
misconceptions.correct: Many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
misconceptions.misconception: Plant cells lose the ability to differentiate at an early stage, in the same way as animal cells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn the pattern for animal cells first and apply it to every organism, without noticing that the specification separates plants from animals here.
misconceptions.correction: Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage, whereas many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.

misconceptions.question: Does cell division still take place in a mature animal?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. In mature animals cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.
misconceptions.misconception: Once an animal is fully grown its cells stop dividing, because cell division is only there to make the animal grow.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cell division is introduced as the way organisms grow, so students tie it to growth alone and expect it to stop when growth stops.
misconceptions.correction: In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

misconceptions.question: Why can an electron microscope show sub-cellular structures that a light microscope cannot?
misconceptions.correct: It has much higher magnification and much higher resolving power than a light microscope.
misconceptions.misconception: An electron microscope shows finer detail simply because it magnifies more, so magnifying a light microscope image further would show the same structures.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnification is the quantity students calculate, so it is the familiar idea; resolution is not calculated and is easily left out of the explanation.
misconceptions.correction: An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope. This means that it can be used to study cells in much finer detail, and it has enabled biologists to see and understand many more sub-cellular structures.

misconceptions.question: How is the real size of an object worked out from a magnified image?
misconceptions.correct: Size of real object = size of image / magnification, with both sizes in the same units.
misconceptions.misconception: Real size is worked out by multiplying the size of the image by the magnification.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that magnification makes things larger and so multiply by it, instead of rearranging magnification = size of image / size of real object.
misconceptions.correction: magnification = size of image / size of real object, so size of real object = size of image / magnification. The image size and the real size must be measured in the same units.

misconceptions.question: One bacterium divides once every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 2 hours?
misconceptions.correct: 64, because there are 6 divisions in 2 hours and the population doubles at each one (2⁶ = 64).
misconceptions.misconception: The population goes up by the same amount at each division, so you can add on, or multiply by a number taken from the question.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the growth as a pattern that rises in equal steps, and reach for a single addition or multiplication using the numbers printed in the question, because that is the arithmetic a rate usually needs.
misconceptions.correction: Bacteria multiply by simple cell division (binary fission) as often as once every 20 minutes if they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature. Each division doubles the population, so after n divisions the number of bacteria is the starting number × 2ⁿ.

misconceptions.question: At what temperature should cultures be incubated in a school laboratory?
misconceptions.misconception: Cultures should be incubated at 37°C so that the bacteria grow as quickly as possible.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that 37°C is human body temperature and that bacteria grow well at it, and they assume the aim of the investigation is the fastest possible growth.
misconceptions.correction: In school and college laboratories, cultures should be incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C. This reduces the likelihood of growing pathogens that could be harmful to people.

misconceptions.question: Why is a Petri dish stored upside down?
misconceptions.correct: So that condensation collecting on the lid cannot drip onto the surface of the agar gel.
misconceptions.misconception: The dish is turned over so that the agar gel cannot fall out and so that the lid is held on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a mechanical reason for turning a dish over, rather than thinking about where the water from condensation collects.
misconceptions.correction: The lid of the Petri dish should be secured with adhesive tape and the dish stored upside down. Storing it upside down keeps condensation on the lid away from the agar gel, so the culture is not disturbed and stays uncontaminated.

misconceptions.question: A clear area around a colony is 20 mm across. How is its cross-sectional area calculated?
misconceptions.correct: Using πr² with r = 10 mm, which gives about 314 mm².
misconceptions.misconception: The measurement taken across the clear area is the value to use in πr², so r is the width you measured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The diameter is the measurement actually taken from the plate, so students substitute it straight into the formula without halving it first.
misconceptions.correction: Cross-sectional areas of colonies, or of clear areas around colonies, are calculated using πr², where r is the radius, which is half of the measured diameter.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a bacterial cell is correct?

options.text: Its genetic material is held inside a nucleus.
options.rationale: A student who expects every cell to be built like a plant or animal cell picks the nucleus. In a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell the genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus.

options.text: Its cell wall is made from cellulose fibres.
options.rationale: A student who thinks any cell wall is a cellulose cell wall picks this. A bacterial cell membrane is surrounded by a cell wall, but cellulose cell walls are a feature of plant and algal cells.

options.text: Its width is close to that of a cheek cell.
options.rationale: A student who judges size from diagrams drawn at the same scale picks this. Bacterial cells (prokaryotic cells) are much smaller in comparison with plant and animal cells.

options.text: Its genetic material is a single DNA loop.
options.rationale: The genetic material of a bacterial cell is not enclosed in a nucleus: it is a single DNA loop, and there may also be one or more small rings of DNA called plasmids.

mcqs.stem: A cheek cell is 6 × 10⁻⁵ m wide and a bacterial cell is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m wide. About how many times wider is the cheek cell?

options.text: About 3 times wider
options.rationale: A student who believes bacterial cells are only a little smaller divides 6 by 2 and ignores the powers of ten. The indices differ by one, so a further factor of ten is needed.

options.text: About 300 times wider
options.rationale: A student who adds the indices instead of subtracting them gets an extra power of ten. Dividing 10⁻⁵ by 10⁻⁶ gives 10¹, not 10².

options.text: About 30 times wider
options.rationale: 6 × 10⁻⁵ divided by 2 × 10⁻⁶ is 3 × 10¹, so the cheek cell is about 30 times wider. This is the order of magnitude difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

options.text: About 0.03 times wider
options.rationale: A student who reads 10⁻⁶ as the larger number divides the wrong way round. The more negative index means the smaller length, so the bacterial cell is the smaller of the two.

mcqs.stem: A muscle cell contains large numbers of mitochondria. What is the function of these mitochondria?

options.text: To transfer energy by aerobic respiration
options.rationale: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs. A muscle cell needs a great deal of energy, so its structure includes many mitochondria.

options.text: To make energy needed for contraction
options.rationale: A student who thinks mitochondria create energy picks this. Energy is not made in the cell: aerobic respiration in the mitochondria transfers energy from glucose.

options.text: To join amino acids into new proteins
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the two structures picks this. Joining amino acids into proteins is the function of the ribosomes, not of the mitochondria.

options.text: To store the glucose used in exercise
options.rationale: A student who treats the mitochondrion as an energy store picks this. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration; they are not a store of glucose.

mcqs.stem: Which parts are found in most animal cells?

options.text: Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a cellulose wall
options.rationale: A student who thinks all cells are strengthened by a cell wall picks this. A cell wall made of cellulose is found in plant and algal cells, not in animal cells.

options.text: Cytoplasm, mitochondria and cell sap
options.rationale: A student who thinks animal cells hold cell sap picks this. Cell sap fills the permanent vacuole of a plant cell; the animal cell part that belongs on this list is ribosomes.

options.text: Cytoplasm, ribosomes and mitochondria
options.rationale: Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes, so all three parts listed here are present.

options.text: Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a large vacuole
options.rationale: A student who remembers the vacuole as a general cell part picks this. A permanent vacuole is one of the parts plant cells have in addition to the parts found in animal cells.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about plant cells is correct?

options.text: Their cell walls are found in animals too.
options.rationale: A student who thinks every cell needs strengthening picks this. The cellulose cell wall is a feature of plant and algal cells; animal cells do not have one.

options.text: Their cell walls are made of cellulose.
options.rationale: Plant and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell.

options.text: Their chloroplasts are in every plant cell.
options.rationale: A student who has only met leaf cells picks this. Plant cells often have chloroplasts, but cells such as root hair cells receive no light and do not contain them.

options.text: Their vacuoles are found in animals too.
options.rationale: A student who treats the vacuole as a general cell part picks this. The permanent vacuole filled with cell sap is one of the parts plant cells have in addition to animal cell parts.

mcqs.stem: A plant cell is 0.06 mm long. On a drawing of the cell, the nucleus is about one tenth of the length of the cell. What is the best estimate of the real diameter of the nucleus?

options.rationale: A student who loses one power of ten leaves the answer unchanged. This is the length of the whole cell, so it cannot also be the diameter of a structure inside it.
A student who divides by 100 rather than 10 shifts the answer by an extra power of ten. One tenth of 0.06 mm is 0.006 mm.

options.text: 0.6 mm
options.rationale: A student who multiplies by the scale factor instead of dividing picks this. It would make the nucleus ten times longer than the whole cell that contains it.
The estimate from the drawing is that the nucleus is one tenth of the cell length, so its real diameter is 0.06 mm / 10 = 0.006 mm. This judges the relative size of a sub-cellular structure.

mcqs.stem: Root hair cells have a long, thin extension that reaches out into the soil. How does this help the cell to carry out its function?

options.text: It makes the cell larger so it can work faster.
options.rationale: A student who thinks specialisation is about size picks this. A cell is specialised by the sub-cellular structures and shape that suit its function, not by being larger.

options.text: It exposes the chloroplasts to more sunlight.
options.rationale: A student who expects chloroplasts in every plant cell picks this. Root hair cells are in the soil, receive no light and do not contain chloroplasts.

options.text: It allows a thicker cellulose wall to form.
options.rationale: A student who treats the cellulose cell wall as the answer to every plant cell question picks this. The cell wall strengthens the cell; it is not what the extension is for.

options.text: It increases the surface area for absorption.
options.rationale: The structure of the root hair cell relates to its function in the plant: the extension gives a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about cell differentiation is correct?

options.text: Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage.
options.rationale: As an organism develops, cells differentiate to form different types of cell, and most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage.

options.text: Most plant cells differentiate at an early stage.
options.rationale: A student who applies the animal pattern to plants picks this. Many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.

options.text: Most cells differentiate by growing to a bigger size.
options.rationale: A student who judges specialisation by shape and size picks this. As a cell differentiates it acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function.

options.text: Most animal cells differentiate to repair damage.
options.rationale: A student who thinks nothing happens in a grown animal except repair picks this. It is cell division in mature animals that is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

mcqs.stem: In a mature animal, what is cell division mainly used for?

options.text: Cell division has stopped in mature animals.
options.rationale: A student who links cell division to growth alone picks this. Cell division continues in mature animals, although it is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

options.text: Cell division makes the cells grow larger.
options.rationale: A student who confuses growth of a cell with division picks this. Cell division produces new cells; a cell changes its sub-cellular structures when it differentiates.

options.text: Cell division repairs and replaces cells.
options.rationale: In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

options.text: Cell division continues as the animal grows.
options.rationale: A student who ties cell division to growth picks this, but the animal in the question is mature. In mature animals, division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

mcqs.stem: Why can an electron microscope be used to study cells in much finer detail than a light microscope?

options.text: It magnifies the image very many more times.
options.rationale: A student who explains detail by magnification alone picks this. Higher magnification on its own gives a larger image, not a clearer one.

options.text: It has higher magnification and resolution.
options.rationale: An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope, so it can be used to study cells in much finer detail.

options.text: It finds the real size from the image size.
options.rationale: A student who confuses the magnification calculation with what the microscope does picks this. Working out a real size is a calculation, not the reason finer detail is seen.

options.text: It uses a much stronger lens to enlarge cells.
options.rationale: A student who treats stronger magnification as the whole answer picks this. The key difference is in magnification and resolution together.

mcqs.stem: The image of a cell is 10 mm wide. The real cell is 0.05 mm wide. What is the magnification?

options.rationale: A student who uses real size = image size × magnification divides the wrong way round. A magnification below one would mean the image is smaller than the real cell.
A student who misplaces a power of ten when dividing by 0.05 gets an answer ten times too large. 10 / 0.05 is 200.
A student who divides by 0.5 instead of 0.05 loses a power of ten. The real width is five hundredths of a millimetre.
magnification = size of image / size of real object = 10 mm / 0.05 mm = 200. Both measurements are in the same units, so the magnification has no units.

mcqs.stem: One bacterium divides once every 20 minutes. How many bacteria will there be after 2 hours?

options.text: 12 bacteria
options.rationale: A student who multiplies the 6 divisions by 2 picks this. Each division doubles the whole population rather than adding two cells.

options.text: 64 bacteria
options.rationale: There are 6 divisions in 2 hours at one division every 20 minutes, and the population doubles each time, so the number is 1 × 2⁶ = 64.

options.text: 7 bacteria
options.rationale: A student who adds one bacterium per division picks this. Binary fission doubles the number present, so the increase gets larger each time.

options.text: 120 bacteria
options.rationale: A student who thinks the population goes up by a fixed amount each division takes that amount from the 20 in the question, giving 6 × 20. Each division doubles the population instead.

mcqs.stem: One bacterium divides once every 20 minutes. What is the number of bacteria after 5 hours, expressed in standard form?

options.rationale: A student who adds one bacterium per division reaches 16. Each of the 15 divisions doubles the population instead of adding to it.
A student who multiplies the 15 divisions by 2 reaches 30. Doubling 15 times gives 2¹⁵, which is far larger.
5 hours gives 15 divisions, so the number is 2¹⁵ = 32 768, which is 3.3 × 10⁴ to two significant figures in standard form.
A student who writes a negative index picks this. A negative index gives a number smaller than one, but the population has grown to tens of thousands.

mcqs.stem: Why should cultures be incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C in a school laboratory?

options.text: It reduces the growth of harmful pathogens.
options.rationale: In school and college laboratories cultures are incubated at a maximum of 25°C, because this reduces the likelihood of growing pathogens that could harm people.

options.text: It is the temperature for fastest growth.
options.rationale: A student who assumes fast growth is the aim picks this. Many bacteria grow faster at higher temperatures, which is exactly why the limit is set.

options.text: It stops condensation forming on the lid.
options.rationale: A student who mixes up the reasons for the safety rules picks this. Condensation is dealt with by storing the dish upside down, not by the incubation temperature.

options.text: It matches the body temperature of humans.
options.rationale: A student who reaches for 37°C picks this. Human body temperature is the temperature the limit of 25°C is set to avoid.

mcqs.stem: Why is a Petri dish stored upside down after the agar gel has been inoculated?

options.text: To stop the agar falling out of the dish.
options.rationale: A student who looks for a mechanical reason picks this. The agar gel is set and stays in the base of the dish whichever way up it is stored.

options.text: To stop condensation dripping onto the agar.
options.rationale: With the dish upside down, condensation collects on the lid below the agar gel and cannot drip onto its surface, so the culture stays uncontaminated.

options.text: To keep the culture warm enough to grow.
options.rationale: A student who focuses on growing the culture quickly picks this. The temperature of the culture is set by the incubator, not by which way up the dish is.

options.text: To hold the lid firmly against the agar.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the dish is inverted to hold it together picks this. The lid is held in place by the adhesive tape, not by the dish being upside down.

mcqs.stem: A clear area around a colony on an agar plate is 20 mm across. What is its cross-sectional area?

options.text: 314 mm²
options.rationale: The radius is half of 20 mm, so r = 10 mm and the cross-sectional area is πr² = π × 10² = 314 mm².

options.text: 1257 mm²

options.text: 63 mm²
